overview.title: A miniature GRU character language model
overview.main_topic: Listing 15.4 (Embedding 256 -> GRU 1024 with return_sequences -> Dropout -> per-step softmax over 67 characters), its 4,024,131-parameter summary, and why language modeling is many simultaneous classification problems (6,400 labels per batch)
overview.central_idea: A character language model is just a sequence classifier that makes one softmax prediction per time step: at each of the 100 positions it outputs a probability distribution over the 67-token vocabulary for the next character, trained with sparse categorical cross-entropy averaged over positions and batch.
overview.importance: This model is the first generative model of the text chapters and the template for everything that follows: the same next-token setup, with a Transformer instead of a GRU, becomes the mini-GPT of chapter 16.
learning_objectives: Read Listing 15.4 and explain each layer's role and output shape
Explain why return_sequences=True is needed for language modeling
Explain why language modeling is still a classification problem
Explain how Keras averages loss and accuracy over 64 x 100 = 6,400 predictions
prerequisites: Character tokenization and the shifted (x, y) pairs (p.447-448)

summary:
**Listing 15.4** defines the miniature language model. With `embedding_dim = 256` and `hidden_dim = 1024`:

1. `layers.Input(shape=(sequence_length,), dtype="int", name="token_ids")`: 100 character IDs.
2. `Embedding(vocabulary_size, embedding_dim)`: each of the 67 tokens becomes a 256-d vector.
3. `GRU(hidden_dim, return_sequences=True)`: a 1,024-unit GRU that returns its output at **every** step, not just the last.
4. `Dropout(0.1)`.
5. `Dense(vocabulary_size, activation="softmax")`: applied at each step, it "outputs a probability distribution over all potential tokens in our vocabulary" (callout).

`model.summary()` shows output shapes (None, 100) -> (None, 100, 256) -> (None, 100, 1024) -> (None, 100, 67) and parameter counts **17,152** (Embedding), **3,938,304** (GRU) and **68,675** (Dense), for a total of **4,024,131 parameters (15.35 MB)**, all trainable. Almost 98% of the parameters are in the GRU.

The model outputs a softmax probability for every character and is compiled with a cross-entropy loss. The authors stress that it is **still a classification problem**; it just makes one classification prediction per token of the sequence. A batch of 64 samples of 100 characters means **6,400 individual labels**. Keras's reported loss and accuracy are averaged first across each sequence, then across the batch.

**Listing 15.5** begins: `model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="sparse_categorical_crossentropy", ...)`. It continues on p.450 with `sparse_categorical_accuracy` and `model.fit(training_data, epochs=20)`, after which the model predicts the next character about 70% of the time.

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s take a look at our model summary:
paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduces the model summary printed below Listing 15.4.
paragraphs.what_it_means: The summary confirms the shapes: the time axis (100) is preserved through every layer because the GRU returns full sequences and Dense acts on the last axis only. Parameters: Embedding $67\times256=17{,}152$; GRU $3\times(256\cdot1024+1024\cdot1024+2\cdot1024)=3{,}938{,}304$; Dense $1024\times67+67=68{,}675$.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Reading shapes and counts is the quickest way to verify that a sequence-to-sequence-shaped model does what you intend, i.e. predicts at every position.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: Keras's GRU defaults to reset_after=True, which uses two bias vectors per gate (input and recurrent), hence the $2\cdot1024$ term per gate. The three gates/candidates are update, reset and the new candidate state.

terminology.meaning: The recurrent layer outputs its hidden state at every time step: shape (batch, steps, units) instead of (batch, units).

connections: p.448: why a GRU was chosen (fast, simpler state than an LSTM)

paragraphs.excerpt: This model outputs a softmax probability for every possible character in our vocabulary,
paragraphs.what_it_says: The model outputs a softmax over the vocabulary and is compiled with cross-entropy. It is still a classification problem, but with one prediction per token: 6,400 labels for a batch of 64 x 100. Reported loss and accuracy are averaged across each sequence, then across each batch.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each position $t$ is a 67-way classification whose label is character $t+1$ of the text (the labels are the inputs shifted by one, p.447). Because the GRU only passes information forward, the prediction at $t$ depends only on characters $1..t$, so it really estimates $p(c_{t+1}\mid c_1,\dots,c_t)$. Averaging means the loss is the mean negative log-probability of the true next character over all 6,400 positions.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Framing generation as repeated classification is what makes language models trainable with the same tools used throughout the book, and it is the foundation of every LLM.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Since every sequence has the same length (100) and no masking is used, averaging per sequence then per batch equals the plain mean over all 6,400 predictions.

terminology.meaning: Cross-entropy where the label is an integer class ID rather than a one-hot vector.
A model of the probability of the next token given past tokens.

connections: p.447: labels are inputs offset by one character
p.452: replacing the GRU with Bidirectional(GRU) would let it cheat by seeing the next token

paragraphs.excerpt: Let’s go ahead and train our language model.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Introduces Listing 15.5, which compiles with Adam and sparse categorical cross-entropy (continued on p.450).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Integer labels from the tokenizer can be used directly with the sparse loss; no one-hot encoding of 67 classes per position is needed.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The compile/fit loop is the standard one; nothing special is needed for language modeling beyond per-step outputs.
connections: p.450: rest of Listing 15.5, 20 epochs, ~70% next-character accuracy

concepts.name: Character-level language model
concepts.definition: A model that, at each position, predicts a probability distribution over the next character given all previous ones.
concepts.technical: Outputs shape (batch, 100, 67); trained with sparse categorical cross-entropy against the input shifted by one.
concepts.significance: Self-supervised (labels come from the text itself) and the basis for text generation (p.450).
concepts.example: Given 'To be or not to b', a good model puts high probability on 'e'.
concepts.misconception: It is not a new kind of learning problem; it is ordinary classification repeated at every step.

concepts.name: return_sequences
concepts.definition: Recurrent-layer option to output the hidden state at every time step.
concepts.intuition: Instead of a single summary at the end, you get a running commentary.
concepts.significance: Required to make one prediction per token.
concepts.example: Without it, the output is (None, 1024) and only one next character could be predicted.
concepts.misconception: It does not make the layer bidirectional or let it see the future.

concepts.name: GRU layer
concepts.definition: Gated recurrent unit: a recurrent layer with update and reset gates and a single state vector.
concepts.intuition: A lighter LSTM with no separate cell state.
concepts.technical: Parameters $3(d_{in}h + h^2 + 2h)$ with Keras's default reset_after=True.
concepts.significance: Fast and holds 98% of this model's parameters.
concepts.misconception: GRUs are not strictly worse than LSTMs; they are often comparable.

concepts.name: Per-step softmax output
concepts.definition: A Dense layer with softmax applied independently at every time step.
concepts.intuition: 67 probabilities summing to 1 at each position.
concepts.technical: Dense acts on the last axis, sharing the same weights across all 100 positions.
concepts.significance: Defines the predicted next-character distribution, later sampled during generation.
concepts.misconception: Dense does not mix information across time steps.

math.title: Next-character prediction at every position
math.source_text: This model outputs a softmax probability for every possible character in our vocabulary

variables.meaning: GRU output at step t (1,024-d), after dropout

math.operations: Affine map then softmax at each step, with weights shared across steps.
math.purpose: Formalizes 'one classification prediction for every token'.
math.interpretation: Because the GRU is unidirectional, $h_t$ only sees $c_1..c_t$, so $\hat p_t$ is a genuine next-token prediction.
math.intuition: The same small classifier reads the GRU's running summary at each step.

math.title: Loss averaged over 6,400 predictions
math.source_text: averaged first across each sequence and, second, across each batch

variables.meaning: true next-character ID for sample i at step t

math.operations: Negative log-likelihood of the correct class, averaged over time then batch.
math.purpose: The sparse categorical cross-entropy objective in Listing 15.5.
math.interpretation: Equivalent to the mean over all $BT=6{,}400$ predictions here.
math.intuition: Each character in the batch is a small exam question; the loss is the average penalty.
math.numerical_example: A uniform guess gives $-\log(1/67) \approx 4.20$ nats per character. If the model gives the true character probability 0.5 on average (geometrically), the loss is $\log 2 \approx 0.69$.

math.title: GRU parameter count
math.operations: Three gate/candidate blocks, each with input kernel, recurrent kernel and two biases.
math.interpretation: The $h^2$ recurrent term (1,048,576 per block) dominates.
math.intuition: Doubling hidden_dim roughly quadruples the GRU size.

code.title: Building a miniature language model
code.original_code:
embedding_dim = 256
hidden_dim = 1024

inputs = layers.Input(shape=(sequence_length,), dtype="int", name="token_ids")
x = layers.Embedding(vocabulary_size, embedding_dim)(inputs)
x = layers.GRU(hidden_dim, return_sequences=True)(x)
x = layers.Dropout(0.1)(x)
outputs = layers.Dense(vocabulary_size, activation="softmax")(x)
model = keras.Model(inputs, outputs)
code.what_it_does: Defines an Embedding -> GRU -> Dropout -> softmax model that predicts the next character at each of 100 positions.

line_explanations.explanation: Integer input of length sequence_length (100), named token_ids.
Per-step softmax over the 67 tokens (callout: a probability distribution over all potential tokens).

code.theory_link: Estimates $p(c_{t+1}\mid c_{\le t})$ at each step.

parameters.name: hidden_dim
parameters.role: GRU state size (1024); also reused for the generation model on p.450.

pitfalls: Forgetting return_sequences=True gives one output per sequence and a shape mismatch with the (batch, 100) labels.
Using a Bidirectional GRU would leak future characters (p.452).

deeper.title: Where the 4 million parameters go
deeper.body:
| Layer | Params | Share |
|---|---|---|
| Embedding | 17,152 | 0.4% |
| GRU | 3,938,304 | 97.9% |
| Dense | 68,675 | 1.7% |

With a tiny 67-token vocabulary, the input and output layers are cheap; the recurrent layer is everything. Contrast the word-level models of chapter 14, where the 30,000-word embedding dominated.

deeper.title: Why one sequence gives 100 training examples
deeper.body: For a chunk 'ROMEO:' with labels 'OMEO: ' (shifted by one), position 1 learns R->O, position 2 learns RO->M, position 3 learns ROM->E, and so on. A single forward pass of the GRU produces all these predictions at once, so a batch of 64 chunks yields 6,400 supervised examples at the cost of one sequential pass.

deeper.title: Analogy: a typist guessing ahead
deeper.body: Imagine a typist who, after every keystroke, writes down a guess for the next letter. Grading every guess (not just the last one) gives 100 grades per line of text; the loss is the average grade.

misconceptions.claim: A language model needs a special non-classification loss.
misconceptions.correction: It uses ordinary sparse categorical cross-entropy, applied at every position.

misconceptions.claim: The model only predicts the 101st character.
misconceptions.correction: It predicts the next character at every one of the 100 positions.

misconceptions.claim: The Dense layer looks at all time steps to make each prediction.
misconceptions.correction: Dense applies independently per step; context comes only from the GRU state.

takeaways: The language model is Embedding(67, 256) -> GRU(1024, return_sequences=True) -> Dropout(0.1) -> Dense(67, softmax).
It makes a 67-way classification at each of 100 positions: 6,400 labels per batch of 64.
Loss and accuracy are averaged over the sequence, then over the batch.
return_sequences=True is what turns a sequence classifier into a per-token predictor.

questions.question: Verify the Embedding and Dense parameter counts.
questions.explanation: Embedding has one 256-d row per token and no bias; Dense has a weight per input-output pair plus one bias per output.

questions.question: Why is return_sequences=True needed?
options: To output a state at every step so a prediction can be made for every token
To reduce the number of parameters
To return the GRU's internal cell state for generation
questions.answer: To output a state at every step so a prediction can be made for every token
questions.explanation: Labels have shape (batch, 100). It does not add a backward pass, does not change parameter count, and returning the state is return_state (used on p.450).

questions.question: How many individual labels does one training batch contain, and why?
questions.answer: 6,400 = 64 samples x 100 characters, one next-character label per position.

questions.question: In what sense is the language model 'still training on a classification problem'?
questions.answer: Each position is a 67-way classification of the next character with softmax and cross-entropy; there are just many of them per sequence.
questions.explanation: The authors' framing: one classification prediction for every token.

questions.question: What loss would a model that outputs a uniform distribution over the vocabulary get?
questions.explanation: Cross-entropy of the true class under a uniform 67-way distribution.

questions.question: Which layer holds most parameters?
questions.explanation: 3,938,304 of 4,024,131. Embedding (17,152) and Dense (68,675) are small because the vocabulary is only 67; Dropout has none.

questions.question: Can you derive the GRU's 3,938,304 parameters from embedding_dim and hidden_dim?
questions.explanation: Three blocks (update, reset, candidate), each with input kernel, recurrent kernel and two biases (Keras reset_after=True).
